doubts: Arcos: the missing War Office document is described differently by sources (a signals training manual from Aldershot on Wikipedia, an air raid document elsewhere). The text says only 'a secret War Office document'.
Arcos: how long the search lasted is 'several days' (Spectator, 21 May 1927) or four days (one secondary source). The text says 'for days'.
Arcos: the size of the police force is not in any source found, so no number is given. Exact date of the break in relations varies (26 to 28 May 1927); the text says 'within days'.

Arcos: how long Soviet high level diplomatic traffic stayed unreadable is put as 'for some time' or 'until the end of the Second World War'. The text says 'for the rest of the years between the wars', limited to high level diplomatic messages (GC&CS did read some Comintern traffic in the 1930s).

Defoe: the flowers at the pillory are reported by the DNB and History Today but are told as 'the story goes'. His cover in Edinburgh (a man fleeing his creditors) rests on one secondary source and the DNB's remark that his plan to settle in Scotland was a pretence; worded softly. The 1718 Delafaye letters are disputed (Furbank and Owens argue he deceived his paymasters), and the text says so. He died 'probably' hiding from creditors, as Wikipedia hedges.
Defoe obelisk: Historic England says readers of the children's magazine Christian World gave at least sixpence each; the text says 'young readers of a Christian paper'.

Cable Street: crowd and police numbers vary widely (100,000 to 500,000; 6,000 to 10,000 police). The text uses 'at least a hundred thousand' and 'thousands of police'. 'They shall not pass' is recorded at Aldgate; the text says it was shouted all day without placing it on Cable Street.

Cable Street picture: no public domain photograph of the battle or the mural was found (mural photos are CC BY-SA). The story uses a 1936 Mosley and Mussolini photo, only 420 px wide; left at native size, not upscaled.
Home: the only public domain views of the Eagle and the Grecian on Commons are 225 to 300 px wide, too small to use. No picture.

Home: Marie Lloyd's first appearance at the Eagle or the Grecian at about fifteen is given as a stage debut by one source and as waitress and table singer by Wikipedia; the text says she 'sings to the customers'.

Asides: Swedenborg's skull is told only as far as the 1978 purchase; whether the skull bought was genuine is itself doubted, so the text says 'what it believed was the real one'. Monteagle letter: authorship unknown, the text says so. Royal Mint embassy: the residents said in August 2026 they would appeal; the text stops at the July 2026 High Court ruling. The Lady Vanishes was also partly shot at Shepherd's Bush, so the text says 'most of'.
Aside streets are guesses: the City part of segment 2 has no aside because the line through the City is not known yet. Every aside has a near point.

Poplar story 2: sources disagree on whether the August 1920 intercepts were officially released or leaked (Jeffery's MI6 history says leaked to the press on 17 August). The text says only that some were 'given to the newspapers'. The jewel sales came out in the press in September, not in the telegrams themselves, so the text keeps them separate.

Poplar story 2: the diamonds in a box of chocolate creams rests on reports of Meynell's MI5 file (National Archives release, 2009, reported by The Times and Stabroek News); the text attributes it to the file. The refusal of the money is credited to the directors, as the Spectator of 18 September 1920 reports, after Lansbury put the question to readers.
Poplar story 2: the number of women jailed in 1921 is given as five (Tower Hamlets panel, OnLondon) or six (Wikipedia), so the text gives no number. The march date (28 or 29 July) is left out.

Poplar story 1: the exact time the school was hit is not in my sources; the text gives only the time the raid reached London (about 11.25). RAF Museum says the children were mostly aged four to six; Historic England says sixteen of eighteen were five or six, which the text uses.

Jolly George: 10 May as the start of the refusal comes from pasttense.co.uk only; Wikipedia gives the sailing date of 15 May. Pollitt as a boilermaker and his later quarter century at the head of the CPGB are from general knowledge, not rechecked this session.

Company's dock: the departure date is 20 December 1606 in Encyclopedia Virginia and 19 December on the monument page; the text uses the twentieth. Settler numbers are 104 or 105; the text says 'about a hundred and five'. 'Behind high walls' is not tied to a cited reason.
Royal Victoria Dock: the raid strength (about 348 bombers and 617 fighters) and deaths (430 to 448) vary by source; the text rounds them. The opening day in 1855 is not given.

Silvertown: the 1917 mill 'on that spot' was the Vernon mill, partly destroyed; Millennium Mills is its 1930s rebuild. The sabotage rumours are presented as not borne out by the inquiry or German records, per History Workshop.

Asides: Blackwall frigates' India and Australia trade and Longplayer's thousand year span are well known but were not rechecked against a second source. Cody Dock as the gasworks coal dock rests on Grace's Guide ('may have originally been St Leonard's Dock') and Cody Dock's own date of 1871.

Route change: segment 6 asides now sit on the Leaway (Albion, Bow Creek loops, Cody Dock and the gasworks). The St Matthias, Millennium Mills and ExCeL Nightingale asides were dropped: St Matthias is at the Poplar stop itself, the mills are in the stop note and the Silvertown story.

Seg 3 has only one aside (Limehouse Causeway); Poplar High Street has none. 'near' points come from the local OSM data in /home/claude/osm/royal-docks except the Albion point, which is an estimate on the Canning Town bank of Bow Creek.
Silvertown story has no picture: no public domain image of the explosion or its aftermath was found on Commons.
Picture poplar-0 (Gotha formation, 7 July 1917) is only 330 px wide: Wikimedia refused the 467 px original (rate limit). Its Commons page calls it public domain, author unknown.

mile-end-0 has no picture: Wikimedia returned 429 for every download after the first few. Suggested public domain file for the master to fetch: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:German_V-1_flying_bomb_in_flight_over_Europe,_in_1944-1945_(342-FH-3A15839-66778AC).jpg (USAAF photo, licence box says public domain). Caption idea: A V-1 flying bomb in flight. US Army Air Forces photograph, 1944.

Grove Road injured: English Heritage and the LRB say 42, Roman Road London says 30; Wikipedia's caption says eight dead against six in English Heritage, LRB and Roman Road. Text says six killed and 'dozens hurt'.

V-1 deception: Wikipedia (citing Masterman, Crowdy, Montagu, R. V. Jones) is the main source for the 18 June decision, Findlater Stewart starting it without War Cabinet approval and Jones's 'fifty per cent or more' estimate. Herbert Morrison's 'who are we to play God' is attributed only by an unsourced site, so it is left out. The text says nobody can measure how far the bombs were moved.

Weizmann at Three Mills: sources say the government gave pilot facilities at Nicholson's Three Mills distillery in 1915 to prove the process, with contamination problems; scale up then went to Holton Heath, King's Lynn and Toronto. Churchill's 'thirty thousand tons' is Weizmann's own account and is marked 'by his own account'. The acetone and Balfour Declaration link is told as Lloyd George's memoir story and called a legend.
Bazalgette making the pipes bigger than needed is a popular claim; the line was cut from the final text.
Peter the Painter: identity unresolved (Piatkov, Janis Zhaklis per Philip Ruff, or perhaps no single man). Text says one historian believes Zhaklis and others doubt he was there or existed.
Gardstein: sources say he was wounded in the Houndsditch shooting; some popular accounts say by a comrade's bullet. Text says only 'is hit too'.

Spare bethnal-green story: National Archives says the Dunne report was published after a statement on 19 January 1945 (22 months); Wikipedia also says results were not released until 1946. Text follows the National Archives. No picture looked for, as instructed.
Bow Bridge date: Wikipedia gives 1110, the Stratford Langthorne article 1177. Aside says 'the story goes' and 'early in the twelfth century'.
Gandhi aside: sources say he walked along the Lea and the canals at dawn from Kingsley Hall; the Sewerbank walks are mentioned too, but the aside now sits on the Lea.
The Irons aside: West Ham United at the Olympic stadium since 2016 and Thames Ironworks building warships at Leamouth are well known but were not fetched again after the route change.
review: Every story and aside was fact checked on 17 Nov 2026 by agents that did not write it; the findings and what was changed are in docs/build/iteration-4-rounds.md.
